tb21_profile.skill: Cross-compile an existing C project for a foreign architecture: obtain/select a MIPS toolchain, retarget doomgeneric's Makefile to it, swap in the provided platform backend, satisfy libc/syscall and static-linking constraints, and iterate on build and runtime failures until the ELF actually executes under a third-party emulator.
tb21_profile.domain: GNU cross toolchains, Makefiles, ELF and MIPS, C portability, emulators (a JS MIPS VM rather than qemu).
tb21_profile.task_form: Build/packaging: take source that does not build for the target and make it build and run there.

searches: tools.py search tmax 'fix the (broken )?Makefile|build (fails|is broken|from source)|undefined reference|linker error|compile the (project|source|library)|\./configure|CMakeLists|ELF (binary|executable|header)|freestanding|libc' -n 26

TMax-15K.reason: The build script compiles the C dependency with the host compiler instead of the cross-compiler and fails to link; fix it to cross-build a static archive for the target. Same bug, same fix.
A backend compiled for a foreign architecture must run under a user-mode emulator; debug why the emulated binary fails and hangs. Cross-build plus run-under-emulator.
Extend a Makefile with conditional cross-compilation that selects the cross gcc per target and names the output per architecture. Exactly the Makefile edit needed here.
A Makefile with a cross-compiler hardcoded breaks the build; diagnose the wrong toolchain selection and repoint it. The mirror image of this task.
Produce both a native binary and a WebAssembly/WASI module from the same source. One source tree, two very different targets.
Build for a musl static target rather than the host default, then actually run the produced binary. Static-linking for a non-default target.
Cross-compile with CGO enabled for two architectures, installing the cross gcc packages needed. Toolchain acquisition plus cross-build.
Add a conditional cross-build flag to CMakeLists that switches to the aarch64 cross g++. Build-system retargeting, in CMake.
Choose the right cross-compiler for a named architecture, compile with it, and inspect the generated assembly. Toolchain selection per target.
Cross-compile one source tree into binaries for two different OS/arch targets from a single build. Basic multi-target build discipline.

Recursive-Task-Synthesis.reason: Build for a foreign arch, confirm with file that the ELF really is that arch, run it under QEMU and check the captured output. Same build-verify-emulate loop.
Write a Makefile driving the cross assembler and linker, then run the result under a static user-mode emulator to produce the expected output.
Discover the available toolchain, implement a Makefile with test and verify targets that check the binary's architecture, and iterate until both pass.
Work through cross-build failures with no external libraries available and record each error hit. The debugging half of retargeting a build.
Several assemblers and linkers are installed; inspect them, pick the correct cross pair for the target, and justify the choice. Toolchain identification.
Build a C library statically for a non-native target, link an application against it, and produce an artifact that node runs. Structurally the same as this task.
Install a vendor cross-toolchain, wire it into the environment persistently, and prove the cross gcc reports the expected target. Getting a cross-compiler usable at all.
Makefile-driven cross assemble-and-link, then run under the installed emulator and post-process the captured output.
Install a cross toolchain and unpack its sysroot into exactly the layout the compiler expects. Sysroot placement is what makes or breaks a cross build.
Makefile with a clean target producing a foreign-arch binary whose emulated output must match exactly. Standard cross build-and-run.

TerminalWorld-Seeds-Clean.reason: Build a C library statically for a non-native target, link the application against it, and emit an artifact node executes. Same pipeline, wasm instead of MIPS.
Configure a source tree's build with a bare-metal cross-compiler prefix and compile it through. Retargeting someone else's build system to a cross toolchain.
Build binutils as a cross-toolchain for a target triplet with an explicit sysroot and library path. Constructing the cross toolchain itself.
Makefile using the cross assembler and linker, with the produced binary run under a static user-mode emulator to hit an exact stdout.
Take a C file through a full alternative compilation pipeline to a loadable artifact and execute it. Non-native compile then run.
Install a vendor cross-compilation toolchain plus its sysroot so cross builds resolve headers and libraries. The setup step this task depends on.
Step through an ELF parser while it reads a MIPS busybox program header; MIPS ELF layout, from the reading side.
Build an emulator project from source with CMake in a clean tree and package the result. Build-from-source discipline in the emulator domain.
Bootstrap a root filesystem using only a statically linked binary, then install into it. Static binaries and target-root layout.
Run and then replay a guest command under a system emulator, capturing both outputs. Driving an emulator, not building for it.

SWE-Smith-Seeds-Clean.reason: GNU triplet generation is wrong for mips and mips64; the triplet is precisely what selects the MIPS cross toolchain.
GnuToolchain resolves compiler variables inconsistently when cross-building, so CC/CXX point at the wrong binaries. The classic cross-build failure.
AutotoolsToolchain mishandles compiler flags, so custom flags never reach the compile line of a configure-based build.
Wrong standard flags generated for specific compiler versions; getting the exact flag set right for a given compiler is what a cross build hinges on.
Incorrect C++ standard flags for a compiler family across versions; compiler-version-aware flag generation.
GnuDepsFlags emits framework flags on non-Apple systems; producing link flags that are valid for the actual target platform.
Changing the compiler leaves stale compiler subsettings in the profile, so a retargeted build silently keeps old settings.
Profile settings such as arch and compiler are lost when serialized; the profile is the description of the build target.
CMakeDeps mishandles transitive dependencies, so the generated build files omit libraries the link needs.
Build-environment script filenames encode configuration and architecture wrongly; per-target build environment plumbing.

SWE-Rebench-Tasks-Clean.reason: Drive a multi-platform build tool over a project whose C++ sources and bindings sit in different subdirectories. Build-system plumbing for compiled code.
A build backend that invokes CMake to compile native code; failures surface as build output, exactly where this task's failures live.
Pyccel compiles Python to C and links it back; the wrapper must handle a type it currently cannot. Generated-C compile-and-link pipeline.
Another gap in the same Python-to-C compilation toolchain; extending a code generator so its output compiles and links.
Built-against versus runtime native library versions disagree and break external dataset access. Native link-time versus run-time mismatch.
A Cython wrapper around a C parser behaves differently from the C library it wraps; reconciling generated glue with native code.
Behaviour tied to a specific native HDF5 build; debugging a Python package against the C library it was compiled against.
Cross-check a Python implementation against the original Fortran through a compiled bridge; porting fidelity across languages.
Reconcile a reimplementation with the Fortran source it was ported from. Port-correctness reasoning, no build work.
A tool resolves against the wrong interpreter on an aarch64 host; environment and architecture confusion in a build tool.

final_top10.reason: Build uses the host compiler instead of the cross-compiler and fails to link; fix it to cross-build and link a static archive for the target.
Statically build a C library for a non-native target, link the application against it, and produce an artifact node executes. Same pipeline end to end.
A foreign-architecture binary must run under a user-mode emulator; debug why the emulated process fails. Cross-build plus emulator runtime.
Point someone else's build system at a bare-metal cross-compiler prefix and get it to compile through. Retargeting an unfamiliar build.
Teach a Makefile to select a cross gcc per target architecture and name outputs accordingly. The precise Makefile edit this task needs.
GNU triplet generation is wrong specifically for mips and mips64 - the triplet is what names the MIPS cross toolchain.
Build binutils as a cross-toolchain for a target triplet with sysroot and library paths set. Building the cross toolchain itself.
Cross-build, confirm with file that the ELF is the right architecture, run it under the emulator and check the output. Same verification chain.
A Makefile hardcoding the wrong cross-compiler breaks the build; diagnose toolchain selection inside someone else's Makefile.
Write the Makefile that drives the cross toolchain, then run the foreign-arch binary under the emulator for an exact stdout.

notes: Strong task: four of five corpora have real cross-compilation content and the top 10 spans four of them. Recursive-Task-Synthesis is unexpectedly one of the best pools here - it has a large family of 'write a Makefile with the aarch64 cross toolchain, build, verify the ELF arch, run under qemu' tasks, which is the TB2.1 loop minus the MIPS specifics; I kept the six that differ meaningfully (verify target, file/checksum verification, toolchain discovery, recorded build failures, toolchain install, sysroot placement) but they are near-clones of each other, so the merge step should thin them. TerminalWorld's wasm/Emscripten tasks (tw_334878) and Emscripten's RTS twin (rts_task_5dc6d30bea094a078a2adabb) are the closest analogues in the whole pool: statically build C for a non-native target and hand the result to node. SWE-Smith's entire signal is the conan package, whose whole job is generating cross-build toolchains - including one issue literally about mips GNU triplets. SWE-Rebench is the weak corpus: no cross-compilation content at all, only Python packages that build native extensions, so its tens top out at 3. None of the shortlisted TMax candidates were useful - the retrievers matched on 'frame' and 'video' - and every TMax pick here came from my own searches.
